items.title: [ScienceDaily] Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in just five years
items.content_html: Switzerland’s glaciers are disappearing at an alarming rate, losing more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 alone. Some of the country’s most famous glaciers experienced their worst melting on record, while several smaller glaciers vanished completely. Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has disappeared in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.

items.title: [thehindu.com] Pacific waters top 30°C as El Niño tracks toward historic peak
items.content_html:
🌲 🏔️ ✏️

The central Pacific's Niño 3.4 region passed 30°C for the first time in recorded history on Oct. 5, as scientists report record heat accompanying the developing El Niño, a natural climate pattern that alters rainfall and temperature worldwide. Surface temperatures there reached 30.06°C, and the anomaly rose to 3.48°C on Oct. 18 before easing to 3.34°C this week. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center puts the chance of a strong-to-very-strong event at 83%; the World Meteorological Organization projects a peak anomaly of 3.8°C around December. NASA satellite measurements, drawn from a 35-year record, show the current pattern resembles October 1997, with unusually high sea levels and warm water extending east toward South America.

items.title: [straitstimes.com] Europe’s record heat drives €17bn economic loss and strains cities
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Europe’s 2026 heatwaves were linked to an estimated €17 billion loss in European Union gross domestic product from April through September, as well as overloaded hospitals, damaged homes and transport disruptions. Separate peer-reviewed research estimated 50,391 heat-related excess deaths across 854 cities, with about 65% attributed to human-caused warming. The study covered urban areas representing roughly 40% of the population in 30 countries. Britain’s hospitals faced demand comparable to a severe winter virus season, while patients overheated in buildings and heat threatened medical equipment. Wildfires damaged homes, transport systems broke down and cooling equipment failed during the summer heat, according to Bloomberg Economics’ assessment. The European Commission is due to propose its first climate-preparedness law on Tuesday, October 27, encouraging public authorities to consider climate risks in investment decisions. The proposal is not expected to include new funding. The Commission is also preparing a heatwave plan that includes data collection and early-warning systems.

items.title: [insideclimatenews.org] UN climate fund earmarks $20 million in first country allocation
items.content_html: The United Nations’ Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage has earmarked $20 million for Nepal, its first country-specific allocation, after an August flood triggered by an ice-and-rock avalanche. At an extraordinary board meeting on Oct. 22, members invited Nepal to submit a project proposal; the board also set aside $1.6 million for oversight costs. The decision does not release the money, and the fund has set no firm timetable for payment. The allocation is less than 0.5% of Nepal’s estimated $4.71 billion recovery and reconstruction bill. The board is expected to consider its first decisions on other funding requests in December, with up to $350 million available, while 119 countries have submitted 176 requests seeking a combined $2.8 billion. Board members from developed and developing countries also disagreed over whether Nepal’s emergency allocation should influence the fund’s long-term approach.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] GM just did 34,000 years of battery testing in less than a month. Here’s how
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Developing new EV battery technology takes years of research. General Motors, for example, says it’s put a decade of effort into lithium manganese-rich, or LMR, batteries, which aren’t yet in any of their vehicles on the road.

But recently, the automaker says it made a big leap in that work. Using computer modeling, GM was able to virtually test more than 300,000 LMR battery pack configurations, advancing from first concept to formal approval in under a month. 

That represents more than 300 million CPU hours, which would take a typical computer 34,000 years, while running 24 hours a day, to complete, according to GM.

GM is leaning into artificial intelligence and virtual simulations to develop its vehicles. That not only speeds up the time to do testing, per the company, but allows it to test more options, rather than picking the best of just a few configurations. 

Those 300,000 formulations, for example, looked at different chemical combinations, temperature cycling, and other approaches to creating a battery cell, Sterling Anderson, GM’s chief product officer, told Fast Company. 

“If we had not had the luxury of some of these tools, we would have had to sample more sparsely from what was possible,” he says. 

Speeding up vehicle development

GM is bringing this AI approach beyond battery testing and into all areas of its vehicle development, with the aim of slashing the time it takes to develop a car in half. 

Typically, cars are developed within a four- or five-year time frame. That allows a “limited number” of all kinds of tests, Anderson says, from wind tunnel to crash tests. 

“Now in the virtual world, instead of the X crash test that we could have done, or Y prototypes that could go through, we can run X times 100 and Y times 1000,” he says. 

GM is also working to advance its autonomous driving capabilities with real-world and virtual testing. Hundreds of data-collection vehicles are currently driving across the country collecting 1 million miles of data a month, while virtually, GM systems drive more than 3 billion simulated miles a day.

By cutting vehicle development down to about two years, GM also says it can adapt more quickly to external challenges. Many car makers were counting on Biden-era EV tax credits to help their sales, for example, but then the Trump administration cut those credits. 

Tariffs, the war in Iran’s effect on gas prices, changing regulations, and uneasy consumer sentiments have all added uncertainty to automakers’ future product lineups, which may have been in development for years. 

A shorter development cycle “makes you more agile,” Anderson says. 

LMR batteries in the works

GM wants to be the first automaker to deploy LMR batteries, and Anderson says they’re on track to make that happen. 

LMR batteries can have 33% more energy density than lithium iron phosphate chemistry, and use a higher amount of less-expensive minerals (like manganese) rather than more of the most expensive minerals like cobalt and nickel. That allows them to offer more range—potentially more than 400 miles—at a lower cost and lighter weight. 

GM is also preparing to roll out its fourth-generation EV platform, which includes not only LMR batteries but a centralized, upgraded computing system, and new electrical work. 

It will have 30% less wiring than GM’s current EVs and 40% fewer parts in its motors and power electronics, which make it lighter and more efficient. 

GM and LG Energy Solution are working on these batteries as part of a joint venture called Ultium Cells. They plan to start commercial production of the LMR battery cells in the U.S. by 2028, at the Ultium Cells facility in Spring Hill, Tennessee.

items.title: [kqed.org] California warns El Niño storms could expose coastal infrastructure risks
items.content_html: California’s Fifth Climate Change Assessment warns of longer summers, shrinking snowpack and a shorter, more intense rainy season. At-risk areas include Highway 37 near Novato Creek and low-lying San Rafael, where homes and businesses sit close to the shore. Gov. Gavin Newsom declared a state of emergency in September to prepare for El Niño. Federal Emergency Management Agency Administrator Cameron Hamilton told state officials on Tuesday to maintain enough reserves to begin disaster recovery without waiting for federal aid. California is increasing resources for local preparations. The World Meteorological Organization says the developing El Niño’s impacts will continue after its expected peak later this year.

items.title: [lemonde.fr] Conservation union warns 96% of shallow-water reefs risk collapse by 2075
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔭 ✏️

The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classified 96% of the world’s assessed shallow-water coral reef systems as critically endangered, warning that they face an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075. Its first global assessment covered 127 tropical and subtropical reef systems. The risk estimate uses a middle-of-the-road climate pathway projecting 2.7°C of warming by 2100. Based on changes over the past 50 years alone, without future climate projections, 24% of the systems would be classified as critically endangered. The IUCN identified climate-driven heat stress as the most consistent global threat, while overfishing, coastal development, pollution, tourism and storms also damage reefs. The assessment was presented at COP17, the U.N. biodiversity summit in Yerevan. IUCN leaders called for emissions cuts, stronger protection and restoration, and sustained investment in coastal ecosystems and communities.

items.title: [science.org] Study estimates summer heat killed 50,391 in European cities
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Researchers estimate that summer heat caused 50,391 excess deaths across 854 European cities in 2026, the highest toll in their records. They attributed 32,619 deaths to the additional warming caused by human-driven climate change. The study covers urban areas representing about 40% of the population in 30 countries; its authors say the total across Europe was likely higher because it excludes rural areas and a deadly May heatwave. The team from Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine used city-level temperature records and historical links between heat and mortality to model deaths, then compared the observed heat with a climate-modeled scenario without human-caused warming. Heat deaths are often not recorded as such on death certificates, and the estimate is not a count of individually verified deaths. Researchers and public-health specialists have called for warning systems, accessible cooling, urban greening and support for vulnerable residents, alongside reduced fossil-fuel use.

items.title: [ArchDaily] COP31 to Take Place in Antalya, Turkiye, as SP Architects Adapts Former Expo Grounds
items.content_html: The 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) will take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20, under a joint governance model where Türkiye hosts the summit and presidency, while Australia leads the formal negotiations. The conference will bring together national delegations, government representatives, scientists, businesses, and civil society to discuss international climate action, including emissions reduction, adaptation to climate impacts, and climate finance. As countries continue to face the challenges of extreme weather, resource consumption, and the transition to lower-carbon economies, this year's programme includes dedicated discussions on zero waste, energy and transport, and resilient cities. In preparation for the event, SP Architects is adapting the former EXPO 2016 grounds in Antalya to accommodate the conference, with plans for the site to remain in use after it concludes.

items.title: [scimex.org] UN warns record El Niño could disrupt weather into 2027
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🌲 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations’ weather agency, warned Oct. 21 that the developing El Niño could push sea-surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific to 3.8°C above average from November through January, with a peak around December. The agency said that level would exceed anything in its four decades of monitoring records. El Niño can shift global rainfall patterns, bringing drought to some areas and heavy rain, floods and heat to others. The WMO expects risks across Latin America, eastern and southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific. Extreme weather has already been reported and could compound humanitarian emergencies. UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said about 50 million people could face increased hunger. He said he had released $50 million for 11 countries and called on governments and development finance institutions to fund preparations before damage occurs. The event is forecast to peak late in 2026, but its effects may persist into 2027 and beyond. Scientists say regional consequences vary: El Niño is a natural climate pattern, but its interaction with human-caused warming and other ocean conditions can influence its effects. Forecasts cannot reliably predict individual storms months in advance.

items.title: [phys.org] Full-scale wave test shows salt marshes can buffer coastal storms
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Researchers moved 306 square meters of intact salt marsh into the Delta Flume, a large wave-testing facility in Delft, Netherlands, and exposed it to waves as high as 2 meters. After 21 hours, the marsh surface had eroded by an average of just 7 millimeters, while its vegetation suffered progressive damage. The study found that plants can reduce wave energy by more than 10%, and by as much as 50% on lower-energy coasts with waves up to 1 meter. Their effect declines as waves grow higher and vegetation is lost. Researchers say marshes could work alongside dikes and seawalls, not replace them. A Spanish coastal-engineering expert questioned how well the Dutch experiment applies to other coastlines, citing wave periods and mobile seabeds among other factors.

items.title: [koaa.com] U.S. emissions rise worsens global warming outlook, UN report says
items.content_html:
🎨 🌲 🔭 ✏️

The United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) 2026 emissions assessment says U.S. greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 133 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2025, the largest increase among major economies. The United States accounted for about 70% of the net increase among 124 countries whose emissions grew. The report warns that the world can no longer avoid exceeding the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C threshold and must limit the overshoot. The U.S. increase reflected higher electricity demand and a rebound in coal-fired power generation, while global greenhouse-gas emissions remained roughly level at 58.4 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent. The assessment attributes its worsening projections partly to the United States’ formal withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions. Under existing policies, warming could reach 2.8°C this century; fully meeting national climate pledges would still leave it at about 2.6°C. UNEP says a pathway offering about a 50% chance of limiting peak warming to 1.7–1.8°C and returning to 1.5°C by 2100 requires global emissions cuts of 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025. The next UN climate summit, COP31, is scheduled to open in Antalya, Türkiye, next month.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] The UN’s latest climate change report is spotlighting the U.S., and not for a good reason
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Losing more ground in the fight against climate change, humanity is heading for a hotter world than experts projected last year — and the United States is a big reason for that, a new United Nations report says.

If all the countries do what they promise to reduce heat-trapping emissions, Earth will likely still warm another 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit (1.2 degrees Celsius) above current temperatures, according to Wednesday’s update of climate calculations by the United Nations Environment Programme. That’s about two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit (0.1 degrees Celsius) more than last year’s projections by the same science team.

“This is a worse outcome than expected last year, as a result of the formal withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions,” the report said. The report also blames the United States for increased emissions last year, saying all the other top 20 major economies reduced their carbon pollution or at least slowed the growth in how much carbon dioxide was spewed from the burning of coal, oil and gas.

“In terms of magnitude, the increase in the United States of America (133 megatons of CO2 equivalent) far exceeded that of all other countries and was driven by increased electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation,” the report said. The 124 countries that increased emissions — not counting the 63 that decreased like most European nations — added 189 million tons of carbon dioxide in 2025, and 70% of that increase came from the U.S., according to the report.

The United States is going “hell-for-leather trying to block renewables while actively promoting and subsidizing dirty coal — and its diplomacy is trying to make other countries also pull back on action. It is looking at the fire, denying there is a fire, and then pouring more petrol on it,” said Australian climate scientist Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics that measures countries’ climate fighting plans. He wasn’t part of the U.N. report but like several other outside scientists said it was scientifically sound.

Shooting far past Paris climate goal

The new calculations say that if countries do all they promise in the climate fighting plans they submitted to the United Nations, by 2100 the globe will be 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter than pre-industrial times. If the world continues on its current path — without national promises — it will be 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the last half of the 19th century, the same as last year’s projection.

Both of those temperatures blow far past the goal of less than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and preferably 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) adopted by the 2015 Paris climate pact. The world is now at about 1.4 degrees Celsius (2.5 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times and earlier this year — and again in this report — United Nations officials conceded that there is no way of limiting warming to the 1.5-degree goal that they had embraced. Instead, officials are pinning their hopes of limiting warming to about 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) and then somehow pulling enough carbon dioxide out of the air to lower temperatures back down to 1.5 degrees.

The world is falling “dangerously short” of even those goals, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said, “but we have the tools to change course and pull back from the brink.”

Drastically cutting global carbon emissions — by 18% by 2030 and 69% by 2040 — “is the only way that we can get back to a semblance of a reality that is still largely manageable without major impacts and therefore that makes every sense,” said UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen.

“The report’s message is clear,” said climate scientist Adelle Thomas, vice chair of a United Nations scientific assessment on climate impacts. She wasn’t part of this study. “We know what needs to be done. We have the tools to do it. And delay only makes the challenge more dangerous and more expensive for all.”

An added tenth of a degree of danger

Report lead author Anne Olhoff, director of UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre, said the U.S. policy change will likely add one-tenth of a degree Celsius (nearly two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit) to global temperatures by the end of the century.

“This report shows that America’s retreat isn’t just a political embarrassment. It has real consequences for the planet and for millions of people around the world,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, a climate organization. “An extra tenth of a degree might sound insignificant, but in climate terms it is enormous. It means more dangerous heat waves, more destructive floods, more failed harvests and more lives lost. For vulnerable communities in Africa, already living on the front lines of the climate crisis, every fraction of a degree matters. These are not abstract numbers. They are human lives.”

Hare said that extra one-tenth of a degree pushes an additional 140 million people “into dangerously hot conditions” and increases the odds of the collapse of the Amazon rain forest or ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica. It also would cost the world and shave about $1.2 trillion from the global economy, said University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann.

And the U.S. effect is probably even bigger than what the United Nations calculates because if the world’s largest historical climate polluter doesn’t do much to fight global warming other nations ease off in their efforts too, said Johan Rockstrom, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research in Germany.

“The rest of the world is exhausted when it comes to counting the damage that the U.S. is willingly doing to allies, multilateral structures, economic cooperation, disaster relief,” Australian climate scientist Malte Meinshausen said. “The rest of the world should probably continue to focus even less on the U.S.”

—Seth Borenstein, AP Science Writer

items.title: [climatechangenews.com] UK approves Jackdaw gas field despite acknowledged risk to climate leadership
items.content_html:
🎨 🏔️ ✏️

The UK government approved gas production at the Jackdaw field in the North Sea on Oct. 21, while its own decision document acknowledged the move could weaken Britain’s climate leadership and make it harder to persuade other countries to stop producing fossil fuels. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh gave that concern “moderate negative weight” against the project’s claimed benefits, saying the approval remained compatible with the UK’s climate targets and 2050 net-zero goal. The UK experienced record heat, drought and wildfires this summer. The United Nations has said global emissions must fall by nearly one-fifth over the next four years to limit climate damage. Campaigners argue Jackdaw will add emissions without materially lowering household bills; government supporters say domestically produced gas can displace higher-emission imports. Legal scholar Margaretha Wewerinke-Singh, who led Vanuatu’s legal team pushing for the International Court of Justice (ICJ) climate advisory opinion, said the government’s treatment of its climate obligations misstates international law. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is due to represent the UK at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya next month.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN urges steep fossil-fuel cuts as 1.5°C overshoot becomes unavoidable
items.content_html:
🎨 🪶 🌲 🔭 ✏️

The United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) 2026 Emissions Gap Report says governments must now limit the scale and duration of global warming beyond 1.5°C, rather than try to prevent that threshold from being crossed. Its lowest-overshoot pathway would cap warming at 1.7°C to 1.8°C around mid-century, with about a 50% chance of returning to 1.5°C by 2100. Following that pathway requires greenhouse-gas emissions to fall 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, compared with 2025. The report says existing national climate pledges would cut emissions by only 5% to 8% by 2030 and 11% to 15% by 2035. If current policies continue, warming could reach 2.8°C this century; full delivery of pledges would still leave it at about 2.6°C. The pathway also calls for sharply reducing coal-fired electricity generation and scaling up carbon removal. The report warns that the required reductions are far beyond current plans. Governments are due to discuss climate action at the COP31 summit, scheduled to open in Antalya on Nov. 9.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘For Panama, it is life or death’: how drought is choking the canal that feeds a nation
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Failed rains and a dire El Niño threaten the waterway that sustains the country, with farmers selling cattle to survive

The cattle should be ambling, grazing contentedly, through Robert Delgado’s fields. Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile attempts to avoid the blistering heat. Soon it will matter little whether their appetite returns, for there will be no grass left to graze.

In Azuero, an agricultural region in Panama’s Arco Seco (Dry Arc), the summer is generally relentless and unforgiving. But this year, the crucial rainy season that precedes it – typically from May to December – has brought little rain to parched fields. The watering holes, streams and rivers that farmers rely on have not been replenished, and pastures – the vital source of animal feed during the dry months – have not regenerated themselves.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Stefan Sagmeister’s new shoe designs are actually walking infographics
items.content_html:
Data visualization turns charts, data, and statistics into something easier to comprehend. Turning that data viz into shoes makes the data into a functional conversation starter.

That’s what the Austrian graphic designer Stefan Sagmeister did with two shoes he designed for Ekn, a German footwear brand, that are on view at his exhibition Finally, Something Good at the Paris gallery Gaîté Lyrique through April 2027.

Sagmeister says the exhibition is meant to look at the world over the long term rather than through daily news. Each shoe uses data to tell a story: one about renewable energy, and the other about homelessness. The key to understanding what the shoes say is written in the footbed.

The Bring It On, a multicolored sneaker about renewable electricity, uses data from the Energy Institute’s 2024 Statistical Review of World Energy to inform the relative sizes of color panels on its sides, with each leather panel representing a different energy source. Yellow, the largest color, represents hydropower, followed by black for wind, pink for solar, and red for all other renewables.

“Wonderfully, the shoe is already out of date,” Sagmeister tells Fast Company. “In the 2025 figures, published this summer, solar passed wind for the first time, so today the pink panel should be slightly bigger than the black one.”

His other shoe, Like a Complete Unknown, is a boot that uses circles to represent the relative homeless populations of six countries. The area of each circular appliqué corresponds to the number of people who are living in the streets and public spaces per 100,000 inhabitants, according to OECD data. The biggest circles are for the U.S., at 76, and Germany, at 46, followed by the U.K. (16), France (8), Mexico (5), and Japan (2).

“Countries count differently, so the numbers are not perfect, but Mexico, a much poorer country, reports a fifteenth of the American rate, and a gap that size is not only a counting difference,” he says. Sagmeister volunteered for the Coalition for the Homeless, an advocacy and service organization, and says what stayed with him from that experience was why some countries handle the same problem so much better than others.

The shoes are available for purchase on Ekn’s website. Both retail for more than $300, of which 10% goes either to the climate innovation think tank Future Cleantech Architects or the Coalition for the Homeless in New York, respectively. Sagmeister sees the inherent awkwardness between homelessness data and a boot costing 350 Euros, and says a donation “doesn’t make that go away.” He hopes people will take away that neither the data behind renewable energy nor homelessness is fate.

“When the number of people sleeping in the street runs from two to 76 per 100,000 across six countries,” he says, that shows “it’s about decisions, and decisions can be made differently.”

items.title: [MacRumors] GM Says Apple Wallet Car Keys Coming to These Vehicles
items.content_html:
In a late September press release that we just discovered now, GM announced that it has started rolling out Apple Wallet car key support in select Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC vehicle models, with additional models to follow over time.


Google Wallet and Samsung Wallet will also be supported, with a related Samsung press release mentioning availability in the U.S. and Canada.

GM said the rollout will occur as follows, with model years listed in parentheses.

September–October 2026



  • Cadillac Vistiq (2027)

  • Cadillac Optiq (2026–2027)

  • Cadillac Lyriq (2025–2027)



December 2026



  • Cadillac Escalade (2027)

  • Cadillac Escalade IQ/IQL (2027)

  • Chevrolet Suburban (2026–2027)

  • Chevrolet Tahoe (2026–2027)

  • GMC Yukon (2026–2027)

  • GMC Yukon XL (2026–2027)

GM said customers will see a notification in the "What's New" section of their vehicle's mobile app when digital key support is available.

Apple Wallet's car key feature allows you to use a compatible iPhone or Apple Watch as a vehicle's car key. GM said supported vehicles will automatically unlock as you approach and lock when you walk away. You can also open the vehicle's trunk and turn the climate control system on or off right from the Apple Wallet app.


GM's digital keys use ultra-wideband technology to enable secure, proximity-based authentication, along with Bluetooth. They work with the iPhone 11 or later (excluding iPhone SE 2, iPhone SE 3, and iPhone 16e) or an Apple Watch Series 6 or later.

To set up a digital car key, GM said to first download and sign in to your vehicle's mobile app. Then, while in your OnStar-connected GM vehicle with its physical key fob nearby, follow the prompts on the app to add a digital key to your compatible digital wallet of choice. More details are available in Apple's support document.
